"Biennial" describes something tied to a two-year cycle. It has two closely related meanings, depending on context.

This is the most common use. A biennial event occurs once every two years — it skips a year, then comes back around.

  • Elections for members of the U.S. House of Representatives are biennial: voters cast their ballots every two years.
  • The Venice Biennale, one of the world's most celebrated art exhibitions, is a biennial event — it takes place every two years.
  • Some governments prepare a biennial budget — a financial plan that covers two full years at once, rather than just one.

"Biennial" can also describe something that spans or continues across a period of two years.

  • A biennial training program is one that takes two years to complete.
  • A biennial report covers a two-year period of activity.

In botany (the study of plants), a biennial plant is one whose life cycle unfolds over exactly two years. In its first year, it puts down roots and grows its leaves. In its second year, it flowers, produces seeds, and then dies. Foxglove and parsley are classic examples of biennial plants.

Whether "biennial" means occurring every two years or lasting two years, the common idea is always a two-year span. The "bi-" part signals two, and "-ennial" connects to the word "annual" (year). So biennial = two years.

This is one of the most common mix-ups in English, and getting it right matters.

  • Biennial = every two years (one occurrence within a two-year stretch)
  • Biannual = twice a year (two occurrences within a single year)

These words look nearly identical but point in opposite directions. "Biannual" divides one year into two. "Biennial" stretches across two years.

Example to make it concrete:

  • A biannual health check-up means your doctor sees you twice a year — say, once in March and once in September.
  • A biennial national health survey means researchers study the country's health once every two years.

The word semiannual means exactly the same as biannual (twice a year). Many writers prefer "semiannual" specifically to avoid accidentally being confused with "biennial."

A reliable way to keep them straight: Biennial events are the ones that feel like they take forever to return — because they do. You wait a full two years. Biannual events, on the other hand, show up twice before the year is even over. If you're ever writing something important and feel uncertain, just write "every two years" or "twice a year" — those phrases are always clearer than either word.

• Politics: legislative sessions, election cycles, policy reviews
  • Government and business: budget cycles, audits, compliance reports
  • Art and culture: festivals, exhibitions, and competitions (the "Biennale" in many art events' names is the Italian form of the same word)
  • Science: research studies, population surveys, environmental assessments
  • Nature: plant life cycles in biology and gardening

In everyday use, "biennial" almost always means every two years. The "lasting two years" sense is less frequent and usually clear from context (e.g., a biennial plant, a biennial budget).
